summary: Profiles Internet mail (MIME and extended SMTP) for use as a way to exchange voice messages between voice mail systems. It was experimental and was replaced by RFC 2421, RFC 2422 and RFC 2423.

eli5.summary: Voice mail boxes from different makers could not talk to each other. This tells them to send recorded messages as regular email attachments so they can.

questions: what is voice profile for internet mail
how to send voice mail over email
how voice mail systems exchange messages
subtitle: A standard way for voice mail systems from different manufacturers to exchange messages using Internet email.

tldr.problem: Voice mail systems from different manufacturers use proprietary protocols to exchange voice messages, making it impossible for systems from different vendors to communicate. Organizations are locked into single-vendor voice messaging.
tldr.mechanism: This profile specifies how to use Internet MIME and ESMTP (Extended SMTP) as the backbone for voice messaging, allowing any voice mail system to send audio-encoded messages as standard email attachments to any other system.
tldr.outcome: Voice mail systems can now interoperate across vendor boundaries using standard Internet mail infrastructure, reducing vendor lock-in and enabling seamless message exchange in corporate networks.

today: This RFC is Experimental. RFC 2421, RFC 2422, and RFC 2423 together supersede and refine the specification. Voice mail systems today can exchange messages across vendors using this approach.

sections.title: The Voice Mail Interoperability Problem
sections.content:
Voice messaging systems are specialized computers that interface with telephone switches to provide call answering and voice mail services. Traditionally, messages sent between voice mail systems have been transported using analog networking protocols based on DTMF signaling and analog voice playback. These analog protocols are proprietary to each vendor, making it impossible for a voice mail system from one manufacturer to send a message to a system from another manufacturer.

As organizations grow and use multiple vendors, the inability for voice mail systems to interoperate becomes a significant limitation. The RFC states that the demand for networking such systems is increasing. The goal of the Voice Profile for Internet Mail (VPIM) is to leverage existing Internet mail infrastructure—MIME and ESMTP—to define a standard, high-quality digital protocol for connecting voice mail systems from different vendors.
sections.eli5: Phone companies made different voice mail boxes, and they couldn't send messages to each other. This RFC says use email instead—everyone already has email working on the Internet, so let's send voice messages that way.

sections.title: Voice Message Format and Headers
sections.content:
A VPIM message follows standard RFC 822 email message format with MIME extensions. Key header fields include From (the originator's fully-qualified domain address), To (the recipient's address), Date (when the message was sent), and Message-ID (a unique identifier). The specification requires that the From field include the mailbox address (which voice systems typically represent as numeric identifiers, like phone numbers) and optionally a text personal name.

The specification defines how mailbox addresses are formatted. Rather than alphabetic email usernames, voice mail systems typically use numeric mailbox IDs, often derived from telephone numbering plans (for example, 2145551212@mycompany.com). The RFC recognizes that most voice mail networks rely on numeric identifiers to remain compatible with the telephone keypad. The specification also reserves special addresses: Postmaster@domain (for diagnostics and required on all systems) and Loopback@domain (for loopback testing). These addresses ensure basic interoperability and allow systems to test their connection.
sections.eli5: A voice message is sent as an email with standard headers like From and To. Voice systems use numbers as mailbox names instead of text names, like 2145551212@company. The system must always have a postmaster mailbox.

sections.title: Voice Encoding and Content Types
sections.content:
The specification defines the MIME content types used for voice messages. The default audio encoding is Audio/32KADPCM, based on the CCITT Recommendation G.721 (now ITU-T G.721), which converts a 64 kilobit-per-second PCM channel to and from 32 kilobits per second using Adaptive Differential Pulse Code Modulation (ADPCM) transcoding. This encoding provides good quality at a moderate data rate. Proprietary voice encodings may be used with explicit per-destination configuration, but use of any encoding other than Audio/32KADPCM reduces interoperability.

The specification also defines Multipart/Voice-Message, a new MIME multipart structure that packages the sender's spoken name, spoken subject, and the message itself in three segments. This allows voice mail systems to present the caller's name and subject before playing the message. The specification requires that these segments be sent if available and should be recognized by conforming systems. For encoding binary voice data over email transport, the profile requires Base-64 encoding when binary transport is not available, and encourages binary transport (using ESMTP BDAT) when possible for efficiency.
sections.eli5: Voice is encoded at 32 kilobits per second, a standard compression. The system can include the caller's spoken name and a spoken subject, sent as separate audio parts before the message itself. Files are encoded as Base-64 unless the system supports binary email.

sections.title: Message Transport and ESMTP Extensions
sections.content:
VPIM messages are transported using ESMTP (Extended SMTP). The specification requires support for standard SMTP commands (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT, RSET) and the EHLO greeting that announces extended capabilities. For better performance with large voice messages, the profile recommends support for BDAT (binary data) command for binary transport and the PIPELINING extension to reduce round-trip delays.

Two ESMTP capabilities are particularly important for voice mail. The SIZE capability allows systems to declare the maximum message size they support, critical since voice messages can be quite large (a multi-minute voice message encoded at 32 kilobits per second requires hundreds of kilobytes). The NOTIFY capability enables delivery status notifications, allowing voice systems to report failures in a machine-parsable way that can be delivered back to the user via voice, since voice mail operators cannot read text error messages. The specification also recommends support for the CHUNKING capability to enable binary transport.
sections.eli5: Voice messages are sent using Internet email (ESMTP). The system announces how big a message it can handle. It uses special email features to send binary voice data and to get notifications if delivery fails, so it can tell the user by voice instead of text.

sections.title: Example VPIM Message
sections.content: The RFC includes an example of a fully-featured voice message sent to two recipients. The message includes the sender's spoken name and a voice message body, marked as important and private. The message uses Multipart/Voice-Message content type with a boundary to separate the spoken name audio, spoken subject audio, and the message audio. Each part is encoded as Audio/32KADPCM with Base-64 transfer encoding. Headers include date, importance level, sensitivity (privacy), and message ID. This example illustrates how a voice mail system should structure a message to ensure that recipients can present it properly: spoken name first, subject second, then the message.
sections.eli5: The example shows a voice message from Greg to two people. It has the speaker's name as audio, a spoken subject as audio, and the message as audio. All three parts are packaged together with standard email headers saying it is important and private.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content: This RFC is marked Experimental. RFC 2421, RFC 2422, and RFC 2423 together supersede this specification and update the voice messaging profile with refinements. The basic vision of this RFC—that voice mail systems can interoperate using standard Internet email infrastructure—has proven sound, and voice mail systems today can indeed exchange messages across vendor boundaries using this approach.
sections.eli5: This was an experimental RFC that tested the idea of sending voice mail over email. It was later refined by three newer RFCs. The basic idea—that email can carry voice messages between different phone systems—is still used today.
